« La musique instrumentale a sauvé ma vi: “Instrumental music saved my life,” says Tati au Miel, an audiovisual artist. As a DJ, Tati au Miel has performed more than 300 times in cities around the world. Right now they are in the middle of a tour and are in New York. Last week, Tati was performing in Texas, where they presented a brand new EP titled Le monde fantastique de Tati au Miel Vol I : dans ma peau.
Si le musicien sait faire danser les gen: While the musician knows how to get people dancing with their noize, ambient and industrial sounds, their cinematic work, drawn from personal experience, invites more introspection. It is precisely the experimental genre, which has become their specialty, that had a saving effect on the artist, who just turned 25. “I’m non-binary and fluid, and the way I see life is radical. Instrumental music is liberating, you can create whatever you want.” It has even given them a reason to live, thanks to the support of a local and international community that makes room for everyone. “It’s for everyone,” Tati says of their music.
Ça devrait être normalisé, d’écouter des: “Listening to different sounds should be normalized; wanting to learn more about it can be intimidating.”
L’artiste se tourne vers la musique à l’: The artist turned to music at 18, introduced to it by their roommates, who were amateur DJs. “It was also a reaction to survive, a way to make money. I’d always been interested in music, but I had no training,” says Tati, who found a way to express themself. Becoming a DJ can be an accessible way to get started in music, according to the artist.
« Tout le monde perçoit la musique diffé: “Everyone perceives music differently, and that’s what’s beautiful. Anyone can make music. It’s part of all our lives,” they say happily.
Montréal possède une belle scène électro: Montréal has a great electronic scene. There are events almost every day, and plenty of platforms exist to promote your art. “Looking at it from afar, it’s really a white scene,” Tati observes. But by creating what you want to see, you attract people who are like you. “The more you produce, the more you attract the community of people you want to be with.”
En voyageant aux États-Unis, en Europe e: Travelling in the United States, Europe and Mexico, Tati realized that everywhere, there are people who share their ideas and experiences. To find and build your community, the musician suggests focusing on your own vision, on what you want to bring and how you want to take part, and putting all your efforts in that direction.
Mais, si Montréal est reconnue pour sa s: But while Montréal is known for its electronic scene, recognition first came from elsewhere. Still, it is their hometown that shaped the artist Tati is today. “My sound is so specific and refined thanks to Montréal,” the musician explains. “But it was when I started playing on the international scene that I got recognized and was able to play in Montréal.”
En se lançant dans la musique, Tati y a: When starting out in music, Tati found role models: “It’s thanks to Black artists who make electronic and experimental music that I wanted to make it, and to discover more.” Their soundtracks call out to Tati in a visceral way. “When I listen to their sound, it resonates more with my values, I couldn’t explain it,” they say. Often imitated, never equalled: when it comes to people from the cultures that created it, the essence is there. “My favourite DJs are trans,” adds Tati.
La <em>house</em> et la <em>techno</em>: House and techno originated as Black music. They were first intended for those communities, as well as for LGBTQ+ people. So Tati and other artists are also working to preserve this art and this history. “Considering that most musical genres come from Indigenous and Black communities, it’s not surprising that trans people, non-binary people and women are the ones carrying the torch for this music.” Tati au Miel is also behind Trademark, a collective dedicated to electronic music.
L’artiste suggère également aux musicien: The artist also suggests that aspiring musicians archive their work, for example by putting it on YouTube: “It’s so important that we, Black people, archive our stuff. That’s how we create history, how we pass it on to our children – by being pioneers in our communities.”
En tant qu’artiste noir et queer, Tati a: As a Black and queer artist, Tati has followed a path that hasn’t been without obstacles. “We get ‘tokenized,’ we know when it’s happening. You’re the only person who looks like you on the lineup,” the musician describes. And support didn’t always come from their loved ones, but today, they are well surrounded. “It’s really sad, but over time, sadness turns into resilience. We’re breaking the hateful, transphobic cycles.”
La pandémie a durement affecté les artis: The pandemic hit artists hard, and Tati au Miel was not spared. “COVID made me realize I need to find a stable way to survive and to live,” says the artist, who lives off their passion. Tati is also a clothing designer, and their creations can be purchased<l1> on their website.</l1> On top of their personal artistic projects, which keep them busy, the musician wants to devote more time to film music. “People forget that it’s music producers who do this kind of work,” Tati reminds us. They are largely responsible for what we feel in front of the screen. “In a movie, when there’s a scene with a lot of emotion, there’s sound – or silence. The person who makes that choice, who creates the emotion, is the music producer.”
On crée ces moments », explique Tati. Et: “We create those moments,” Tati explains. And everywhere, we hear this music, which sets the rhythm of our lives. “It’s beautiful that some people pay attention to sound and are able to produce things that make people happy, that make them dance, cry, feel emotions,” says Tati. And it is this healing power that the artist represents, along with that of an artistic community that extends well beyond borders. That is why Tati encourages those who share their experience to chart their own path. “Despite the obstacles, you can’t lose sight of the foundation, which is our reasons for doing what we do.”
